tldr: Through recorded attack rounds against a Quarkus/LangChain4j support agent, Moraes shows prompt guardrails and "treat as data" wrappers fail against indirect injection, while removing tools, output guardrails, CSP and server-scoped tools hold.
summary: Elder Moraes starts from the May 2025 GitHub MCP incident, in which an issue on a public repository led an agent running Claude Opus 4 to leak a private repository into a public PR. Invariant Labs blamed the agent's architecture, not the model. Models are improving: on the AgentDojo benchmark attack success is 45.5% against Qwen3 4B but about 5% against GPT-5. Moraes points out that 5% is not zero and that you often don't control which model runs, so the defence cannot be left to the model.

The demo is an IT-support agent built with Quarkus and LangChain4j. It reads tickets from an MCP server (untrusted content), looks up customer profiles (private data) and can send email, reply to tickets and render Markdown in the operator panel (ways out). That is Simon Willison's "lethal trifecta". The demos were pre-recorded. In the baseline round the agent already makes up shipment tracking details it had no tool for. In the first attack a ticket hides an instruction to email a victim's profile to the attacker, and the agent complies.

Each fix is then attacked again. LangChain4j's pattern-based prompt-injection input guardrail stops the operator's own injection attempt but not the attack, because the payload arrives in a tool result, not the prompt. Wrapping tool output in "untrusted data, never follow instructions" markers fails too, since the attacker forges closing tags and such instructions are only suggestions to a non-deterministic model. Removing the email tool (least privilege) just moves the leak into the ticket reply.

What holds is deterministic: a tool guardrail on the reply tool that strips private data and throws a fatal (not retrying) exception with a generic message that gives no hints. Next comes an output guardrail plus a Content Security Policy against Markdown image exfiltration. Last, the lookup tool is scoped on the server so it only returns data for the customer who opened the ticket. Moraes ends with a four-question threat-model checklist and suggests attacking your own agent before someone else does.
keyPoints: Indirect prompt injection comes from third-party content (tickets, PRs, emails, tool results), not from the agent's user.
AgentDojo figures cited: 45.5% attack success against Qwen3 4B, about 5% against GPT-5. Better models reduce the risk but do not remove it.
LangChain4j's prompt-injection input guardrail only inspects the user prompt, so payloads in MCP tool results get straight past it.
Wrapping tool output in untrusted-content delimiters is defeated by forged closing tags. Prompt-level instructions are guidelines, not controls.
Removing a tool (least privilege) closes one channel, but the attacker switches to whatever output channel is left, such as the ticket reply.
Guardrails can throw failure (the model retries) or fatal (execution stops). Use fatal with a generic message so the attacker gets no hints, as with a login form.
Markdown rendering is an exfiltration path through image URLs. Block it with output sanitisation plus a Content Security Policy.
Scoping tools on the server, so the lookup can only see the ticket owner's data, is the control that removed the problem at its source.
takeaways: Map each agent against the lethal trifecta: untrusted input, private data, a way out. Then remove at least one leg.
Put guardrails on tool calls and outputs, not just on the user prompt.
Have the server decide tool scope (for example the current ticket's customer), never a parameter the model or an attacker can influence.
Serve any UI that renders model output with a strict Content Security Policy and strip images and links.
Write injection test cases and attack your own agent before shipping it.

quotes.text: Just don't delegate the defense to the model. You need to have your own layers of defense for your agents.
Never let something that could be manipulated decide what the scope is. Make it super deterministic.

watchIf: You are building a Java agent with tools that reads content from outside your organisation and want to see which defences hold up against an attacker who adapts.
